Before you start this guide, you should have completed either "02_software_setup_ubuntu.qmd" (for Ubuntu, including Ubuntu inside WSL on Windows) or "02_software_setup_mac.qmd" (for a Mac). Those guides install R, Python, PostgreSQL, Quarto and Positron. This guide installs the R and Python packages we use in the course and sets up Quarto to run R and Python in the same document. From here on, the steps are the same on Ubuntu and on a Mac.

## Convenience Setup

Before we continue, let's set up a convenience: we would like to be able to run lines of bash (linux) in the linux terminal directly from the `qmd` file currently open.

Assuming you're using Positron, we need the ability to send commands from this `qmd` document directly to terminal. (By default this is only enabled for R or Python). So follow these instructions:

Open File → Preferences → Keyboard Shortcuts, or press Ctrl+K and then Ctrl+S.
In the search box, type "Run Selected Text In Active Terminal".
Click the pencil icon next to that command, press the keys you want (for example Ctrl+Alt+Enter), then press Enter. You don't want to use Ctrl+Enter as this will conflict with R/Python later.

Run every command in the terminal. A few commands are too long to fit on one line, so they continue on the following lines, either after a `\` or inside quotes. Copy all the lines together and the terminal runs them as one command.


# Python environment and packages

We will add packages to this guide during the semester. The last section explains what to do when that happens.

Neither Ubuntu nor Homebrew allows `pip` to install packages into the Python they manage (you would get an `externally-managed-environment` error). Instead, create a virtual environment for the course and install packages there:

```bash
python3 -m venv ~/.venvs/bigdata
source ~/.venvs/bigdata/bin/activate
```

Your prompt now begins with `(bigdata)`, and inside the environment the commands `python` and `pip` refer to the environment's own copies. Type `deactivate` to leave it. You need to run the `source` line again in every new terminal where you want to use the environment. Positron looks for environments in `~/.venvs`, so it will find this one on its own.

With the environment active, install the Python packages we use in the course, so that everyone works with the same set:

```bash
pip install numpy pandas polars duckdb pyarrow scikit-learn lightgbm \
  ipykernel "psycopg[binary]" "ibis-framework[postgres]" \
  "xgboost-cpu; sys_platform == 'linux'" \
  "xgboost; sys_platform == 'darwin'"
```

`psycopg` is the PostgreSQL driver for Python (the `[binary]` part, quotes included, selects a ready-built version so nothing needs compiling). `ibis` writes the SQL for you from Python code, and its `[postgres]` part adds what it needs to talk to PostgreSQL. The last two entries, quotes included, are two versions of the same package, and `pip` picks the one for your system. On Ubuntu it installs `xgboost-cpu`, a build without GPU support; the regular build pulls in several hundred megabytes of NVIDIA libraries that only matter when training on multiple GPUs. On a Mac, where no such build exists or is needed, it installs the regular `xgboost`. Either way the package is used as `xgboost` in your code. Near the start of its output, `pip` prints a line beginning with `Ignoring` about the version it did not install, which is expected.

This downloads a couple of hundred megabytes, so it can take several minutes. Check that the packages load:

```bash
python -c "import numpy, pandas, polars, duckdb, pyarrow, psycopg, ibis; print('ok')"
python -c "import sklearn, xgboost, lightgbm; print('ok')"
```

Both commands should print `ok`.

# R packages

Install the R packages we use in the course:

```bash
Rscript -e 'install.packages(c("tidyverse", "data.table", "R.utils",
  "arrow", "duckdb", "RPostgres", "bench", "profvis", "httr2", "digest",
  "future", "furrr", "xgboost", "lightgbm",
  "knitr", "rmarkdown", "reticulate"))'
```

The packages listed need many others, so well over a hundred packages are installed and it takes several minutes. When one package fails, R moves on to the next and only prints a warning at the end, so check that the main ones load:

```bash
Rscript -e 'suppressMessages({library(tidyverse); library(data.table)
  library(arrow); library(duckdb); library(RPostgres); library(xgboost)
  library(lightgbm); library(reticulate)})
  cat("ok\n")'
```

This should print `ok`. If it says `there is no package called` something, look through the output of the install command for a line saying `installation of package ... had non-zero exit status`. That package had to be compiled on your computer and something it needs was missing, almost always a system library. On Ubuntu, the usual cause is having skipped the `sudo apt install` line in the "Prepare R for installing packages" section of the Ubuntu guide; `RPostgres`, for example, needs `libpq-dev` from that line. Run that line, then run the `install.packages` command above again.

# Connecting to PostgreSQL from R and Python

In the earlier guide you saw that `psql` connects without a password. The same is true from R and Python, with one rule: **do not pass a `host`**. Check both:

```bash
Rscript -e 'con <- DBI::dbConnect(RPostgres::Postgres()); print(DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT version()"))'
python -c "import psycopg; print(psycopg.connect().execute('SELECT version()').fetchone()[0])"
```

Each should print a line beginning with `PostgreSQL 18`.

Why the rule: with no `host`, the connection goes through a local socket file and PostgreSQL identifies you by your operating-system username, which is why no password is needed. With `host = "localhost"`, which many tutorials show, the connection goes over the network instead, and PostgreSQL then insists on a password that your setup never created. The error is `fe_sendauth: no password supplied`. If you ever do need a network connection (for example from a program that cannot use the socket), set a password once with `\password` inside `psql` and then pass `host = "localhost"` together with `password`.

# R and Python together in Quarto

A single Quarto document can contain both R and Python code. Quarto runs the code in such a document with R's `knitr` and `rmarkdown` packages, and the `reticulate` package lets R start Python for the Python parts. All three were installed in the previous section.

Left alone, `reticulate` chooses a Python by itself, and it may not be your `bigdata` environment. Packages you installed there would then appear to be missing when you render a document. Tell `reticulate` which Python to use by setting the variable `RETICULATE_PYTHON` in `~/.Renviron`, a file R reads every time it starts:

```bash
echo "RETICULATE_PYTHON=$HOME/.venvs/bigdata/bin/python" >> ~/.Renviron
```

Check the result:

```bash
Rscript -e 'reticulate::py_config()'
```

The first line should read `python:` followed by the path of `.venvs/bigdata/bin/python` inside your home directory. Further down, the `numpy:` line should show a folder inside `.venvs/bigdata` as well, which confirms that R sees the Python packages you installed above.

Let's make sure you have R and Python setup correctly. Here are two chunks that should test it. Go to console on the bottom pane and click the "+" sign to start both an R session. Then click the down icon next to plus and click "start another" and choose the python in 

```{r}
7 + 3 #CTRL+ENTER or click "run cell"
```

```{python}
7 + 3 #CTRL+ENTER or click "run cell"
```

# When the package lists change

When we add a package to one of the lists above, repeat that step:

- For Python, activate the environment with `source ~/.venvs/bigdata/bin/activate` and run the `pip install` command again. `pip` skips the packages you already have.
- For R, run the `install.packages` command again. R installs all the listed packages again, which also brings them up to date.
